title: What training do the EBA internal governance and suitability guidelines require of banks?
description: Training duties in EBA internal governance guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/05 and the 2026 revision) and induction rules in the EBA and ESMA suitability guidelines.
shortAnswer: The European Banking Authority (EBA) expects banks to build risk culture through staff training, give control function staff regular training, and train staff on codes of conduct and business continuity, under its internal governance guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/05). The joint EBA and ESMA suitability guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/06) add induction for board members: key information within one month and induction completed within six months. A revised governance text, EBA/GL/2026/10, was published on November 5, 2026.
keyTakeaways: EBA/GL/2021/05 has applied since December 31, 2021 and contains training expectations for risk culture, codes of conduct, the risk management and compliance functions, all internal control functions and business continuity.

On November 5, 2026 the EBA published revised internal governance guidelines (EBA/GL/2026/10) reflecting CRD VI. As at November 2026 they are final but awaiting translation and apply two months after publication in all EU official languages.
The suitability guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/06) require a board approved induction and training policy, key information for new board members within one month and induction completed within six months.

CRD VI rewrote Article 91 of Directive 2013/36/EU: induction and training of management body members must now include ESG risks and impacts and ICT risk, with national measures applying from January 11, 2026.
Each guideline expects documented policies, identified training needs and an evaluation of training quality, which is what supervisors ask to see.
regulator: European Banking Authority (EBA), applied through national competent authorities that comply with the guidelines
appliesTo: Institutions under Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) and investment firms subject to Title VII of that Directive under Regulation (EU) 2019/2033
Members of the management body in its management and supervisory functions
Key function holders, including heads of internal control functions
Staff of the risk management, compliance and internal audit functions
All staff, for risk culture, code of conduct and business continuity training

sections.heading: Which EBA guidelines contain training requirements?

blocks.text: Two sets of guidelines matter: the EBA Guidelines on internal governance under Directive 2013/36/EU, which cover staff and control functions, and the joint EBA and ESMA Guidelines on the assessment of the suitability of members of the management body and key function holders, which cover board induction and training. Both were issued under the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) and both have applied since December 31, 2021 ([EBA internal governance guidelines page](https://www.eba.europa.eu/activities/single-rulebook/regulatory-activities/internal-governance/guidelines-internal-governance-under-crd)).

EBA guidelines are addressed to competent authorities and institutions. Competent authorities notify the EBA whether they comply or intend to comply, and then apply the guidelines in supervision, so the practical effect for a bank depends on its supervisor's stance. Training expectations in the guidelines are principles based: they say what training must achieve and for whom, not how many hours to deliver.

These guidelines are distinct from the ICT awareness duties under the [Digital Operational Resilience Act](/regulations/dora-ict-security-awareness-training) and from sector specific competence regimes such as the [Mortgage Credit Directive](/regulations/mortgage-credit-directive-staff-knowledge-competence), which apply alongside them.

sections.heading: Which version of the internal governance guidelines applies now?

blocks.text: As at November 2026, EBA/GL/2021/05 still applies. The EBA published the revised guidelines, EBA/GL/2026/10, on November 5, 2026, and its website shows their status as final and awaiting translation into the EU official languages ([EBA press release, November 5, 2026](https://www.eba.europa.eu/publications-and-media/press-releases/eba-publishes-revised-guidelines-internal-governance-delivering-greater-proportionality-and)).

The final report states that the revised guidelines "apply from [two months after publication in all EU official languages]" and that EBA/GL/2021/05 will be repealed from the same date ([final report, EBA/GL/2026/10](https://www.eba.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-11/3c8b1810-c335-499a-803f-6d795ce3d196/Final%20report%20on%20Guidelines%20on%20internal%20governance.pdf)). The revision implements Directive (EU) 2024/1619 (CRD VI), adds a mapping of duties for management body members and key function holders, and introduces governance rules for third country branches. The training provisions carry over with renumbering, as the table below shows.

sections.heading: What do the internal governance guidelines expect of staff training?

blocks.text: The guidelines expect training to serve three governance outcomes: a sound risk culture, conduct in line with the code of conduct, and competent control functions. Paragraph 96 of EBA/GL/2021/05 states that institutions "should develop a risk culture through policies, communication and staff training regarding the institutions' activities, strategy and risk profile" and should adapt training to each person's responsibilities for risk taking and risk management.

items: **Code of conduct (paragraph 104):** institutions should monitor compliance with conduct standards and ensure staff awareness, for example by providing training, and report results to the management body periodically.
**All internal control functions (paragraph 177):** staff should remain qualified on an ongoing basis and receive training as necessary.
**Risk management function (paragraph 182):** staff should have sufficient knowledge of risk management techniques, markets and products, and access to regular training.
**Compliance function (paragraph 207):** staff should have sufficient knowledge of compliance and relevant procedures, and access to regular training.
**Business continuity (paragraph 230):** appropriate training should be provided on contingency, business continuity and recovery plans.

blocks.text: Paragraph 101 also requires gender neutral policies, explicitly including access to training. In practice, supervisors look for a link between the institution's risk profile and the training curriculum, which the guide on [mapping training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) explains.

sections.heading: What induction and training must management body members receive?

blocks.text: Title IV of the suitability guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/06, also ESMA35-36-2319) requires induction covering laws, the institution's structure, business model, risk profile and governance, plus general and individually tailored training. Paragraph 93 sets the clock: "All newly appointed members of the management body should receive key information one month after taking up their position at the latest, and the induction should be completed within six months" ([suitability guidelines final report](https://www.eba.europa.eu/sites/default/files/document_library/Publications/Guidelines/2021/EBA-GL-2021-06%20Joint%20GLs%20on%20the%20assessment%20of%20suitability%20%28fit%26propoer%29/1022127/Final%20report%20on%20joint%20EBA%20and%20ESMA%20GL%20on%20the%20assessment%20of%20suitability.pdf)).

items: **Closing gaps (paragraph 94):** where a member must fill a particular knowledge or skill gap, training should aim to close it within an appropriate timeframe, and in any case the member should meet all knowledge and skill elements no later than one year after taking up the position.

**Policy (paragraphs 95 and 97):** institutions need an induction and training policy adopted by the management body, setting objectives by function and committee role, responsibility for the training program, the financial and human resources available and a process for members to request training.
**Needs analysis (paragraph 99):** a process to identify training needs for the board collectively and for each member, with input from business areas and internal control functions.

**Currency and evaluation (paragraphs 100 and 101):** policies and training plans kept up to date for governance, strategy, product and legal changes, and an evaluation process for the execution and quality of induction and training.

blocks.text: The legal anchor moved under CRD VI. Before the amendment, Article 91(9) of Directive 2013/36/EU required institutions to devote adequate human and financial resources to induction and training of management body members. As amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1619, the paragraph now reads that entities "shall devote adequate human and financial resources to the induction and training of members of the management body, including on ESG risks and impacts and on ICT risk". CRD VI had to be transposed by January 10, 2026 and applied from January 11, 2026 ([Directive (EU) 2024/1619](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024L1619)). The EBA lists the suitability guidelines as under ongoing review, with the consultation closed, as at November 2026.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each governance expectation, such as the induction clock, gap closure within a year and control function training, to the roles and concepts it covers. When the revised guidelines take effect, the renumbered paragraphs are linked in the framework, so evidence and curricula stay traceable without rebuilding the training library.

faqs.q: Are EBA guidelines legally binding on banks?
faqs.a: Not directly. EBA guidelines are addressed to competent authorities and financial institutions, and competent authorities state whether they comply. Once a supervisor applies them, it assesses institutions against them in ongoing supervision, so in practice banks treat them as supervisory expectations that must be met or justified.

faqs.q: Do the guidelines set a minimum number of training hours for board members?
faqs.a: No. The suitability guidelines set time limits for induction and gap closure but no hours. Paragraph 96 of the suitability guidelines says institutions should consider industry benchmarks, such as training budget and training days, including EBA benchmarking results, when deciding the resources for induction and training.

The final report says the revised guidelines apply two months after publication in all EU official languages, with EBA/GL/2021/05 repealed from that date. As at November 2026 the EBA lists them as final and awaiting translation, so no application date has yet been set.

faqs.q: Do the suitability guidelines cover key function holders as well as directors?
faqs.a: Yes. The joint EBA and ESMA guidelines cover the suitability of members of the management body and key function holders. The induction and training provisions in Title IV are written for management body members, while key function holders are assessed for knowledge, skills and experience under other parts of the guidelines.
